title: the Sundered Sea Rising Anew
premise: Kestrel Sterling flees her hedge-witch master into the Stillwater Valley, the one place in the Sundered Sea where magic cannot follow — and where she believes she is finally safe. But a dying cartographer presses a map of Vael, a drowned country that officially no longer exists, into her hands, and its ink binds itself to her blood: she is the last heir of Vael's door-wardens, and only she can open the way out before the dragon-fire that holds the sea back gutters forever. Hunted by the Ember Court's zealots who want the fire extinguished and by her old master who wants the map, Kestrel must choose between sealing herself safely inside the valley or claiming an inheritance that will cost everyone she loves. In the end she rekindles the dragon-fire with her own life-thread, becoming the living door between the drowned country and the world — loved, duty-bound, and permanently changed.
about_author: Ada Crane is the pen name of a former tide-pool surveyor who grew up on a disappearing coastline and now writes fantasy about places that refuse to stay lost. She lives inland, unhappily, with two cats named after shipwrecks.

chapters.title: The Valley That Forgets
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She crosses into the Stillwater Valley, shedding her apprentice name and her magic like wet clothes, and takes work mending nets in the village of Lowmark. The emotional beat is brittle relief — safety that feels suspiciously like erasure.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Tide Gate
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A burned, half-drowned stranger collapses at the tide gate clutching a leather map case; with his last breath he calls her 'warden's daughter' and presses the map into her hands. She feels the valley's numbness crack for one terrible heartbeat. Beat: dread disguised as pity.

chapters.title: Ink That Remembers
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, with a brief interlude from the dying man's memory bleeding through the map. The map's ink crawls onto her skin, showing her Vael — towers, harbors, a mountain with a sleeping heart of fire. Beat: horrified wonder as inheritance becomes literal.

chapters.title: The Zealots of the Ember Court
chapters.summary: New POV: Serah Vane, an Ember Court inquisitor, arrives in Lowmark following the same death-scent, interrogating villagers about a runaway girl. Kestrel watches from the fish sheds, learning her enemy's creed: all fire must gutter so the sea can be whole. Beat: cold fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: What Her Master Taught
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, flashback-heavy. We learn why she ran: her hedge-witch master Maren wanted to use her bloodline for exactly this map, and Kestrel chose cowardice over complicity. Now Maren is on the road behind her too. Beat: guilt reframed — she didn't flee duty, she fled being used.

chapters.title: The Door Out of Nowhere
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Following the map's first clue, she finds a stone arch standing alone in a barley field — a door to nowhere that hums when she touches it. Serah nearly catches her; a village boy, Tam, covers for her and demands answers. Beat: first alliance, grudging and warm.

chapters.title: Salt in the Blood
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. He follows Kestrel against her wishes and discovers the truth of the map; his own grandmother was Vaeli, one of the drowned-country refugees the valley quietly absorbed. Beat: shared inheritance — neither of them is as ordinary as they believed.

chapters.title: Maren at the Crossroads
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Her old master catches up to her, not with chains but with apologies and an offer: come home, let me carry this burden for you. Kestrel sees the hunger underneath and refuses. Beat: love against manipulation; she chooses the hard road over the comfortable cage.

chapters.title: The Drowned Archive
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Tam's alternating POV. Beneath a lake, the map opens a stairway into Vael's flooded archive, where books breathe underwater and a librarian made of coral has waited ninety years. Beat: awe — the dead country is not dead, only holding its breath.

chapters.title: Ninety Years Under
chapters.summary: The coral librarian's POV. A haunting chapter of memory: the night Vael sank, the warden family's sacrifice, the dragon-fire lit to hold the sea back. Kestrel learns what 'warden' truly cost. Beat: grief as education; the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Serah's Doubt
chapters.summary: Serah Vane's POV. Standing in the flooded archive's wake, Serah finds evidence the Ember Court engineered Vael's drowning — her own faith cracks. She burns the orders rather than report them. Beat: the enemy becomes human; conviction turns to crisis.

chapters.title: The Guttering
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Far off, the horizon glows wrong — the dragon-fire is failing, and the sea begins to rise along coasts hundreds of miles away. Refugees flood toward the valley, which cannot hold them. Beat: stakes go global; personal escape is no longer possible.

chapters.title: Three Roads to One Mountain
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, rotating POV. Kestrel, Tam, a reluctant Serah, and even Maren converge on Mount Vael by different roads, each carrying their own reason. Betrayal brews in the camp at night. Beat: uneasy fellowship under pressure.

chapters.title: Maren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. She offers herself to the Ember Court remnant in exchange for Kestrel's safe passage, believing she can outmaneuver them. She cannot. Beat: tragic self-deception; the mentor's love expressed as control, then as sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Ascent
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The climb through Vael's burning terraces, past statues of every warden who came before her — each one a person who gave their life-thread to the fire. Tam confesses he loves her; she cannot answer. Beat: love against duty, stated plainly and left unresolved.

chapters.title: The Last Dragon
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At the caldera she meets the fire's source: not a beast but a dying dragon older than the country, kept alive for centuries by warden after warden. It asks her the question the whole book has asked: what will you pay? Beat: confrontation with the true cost.

chapters.title: Serah's Choice
chapters.summary: Serah's POV. The Ember Court remnant storms the caldera to extinguish the fire forever. Serah turns her blade on her former brothers-in-faith and falls buying Kestrel time. Beat: redemption purchased at full price; the theme of inheritance passed to a stranger.

chapters.title: The Life-Thread
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. To rekindle the fire she must weave her own life-thread into it — not die, but never again be separate from the flame. Tam begs her to stop; she kisses him and steps forward anyway. Beat: climax of love against duty; she chooses, eyes open.

chapters.title: Rising Anew
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The dragon-fire roars back to life; the sea recedes; Vael's drowned streets begin, impossibly, to drain and dry. Kestrel stands in the caldera transformed — warm to the touch, glowing faintly, no longer entirely mortal. Beat: triumph braided with loss.

chapters.title: The Door Between
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She becomes the living door: refugees pass through her arch into reborn Vael, and she greets each one by name, because the map's memories are hers now. Tam stays at her threshold, unwilling to leave. Beat: bittersweet settlement of the love question — together, but changed.

chapters.title: What the Valley Cannot Hold
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Lowmark and the Stillwater Valley must reckon with what they sheltered and denied for ninety years; the valley's magic-numbness breaks, and hedge-witches' abandoned arts stir again. Beat: reckoning — survival was never free, and now everyone pays their share.

chapters.title: A Warden's Ledger
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, epilogue. One year later, she opens Vael's first new archive and writes the first entry in a fresh ledger of wardens — Tam's name beside hers. The dragon sleeps soundly. Final beat: inheritance reclaimed not as burden but as promise, and the sea, rising anew, held at bay.
